mcqs.question: Searching for the first occurrence of a target in a sorted array with duplicates, arr[mid] equals the target. What should happen next?
options: Return mid immediately, since a match has been found
Record mid as a candidate answer, then continue searching the left half (hi = mid - 1) for a possibly earlier occurrence
Record mid as a candidate answer, then continue searching the right half (lo = mid + 1)
Discard this match and continue searching both halves independently
mcqs.explanation: A match at mid doesn't guarantee it's the FIRST match — an earlier occurrence could still exist further left, so the search must continue narrowing toward the left while keeping this position as the best candidate found so far. Returning immediately risks returning a later duplicate, and searching right would look for a LAST occurrence instead, not a first one.

mcqs.question: In the search_range helper function, what is the only difference between the find_first=True and find_first=False calls?
options: find_first=False uses a completely separate algorithm with different time complexity
Which direction (hi = mid - 1 vs lo = mid + 1) the search continues after finding a matching element
find_first=True requires the array to have no duplicates
The two calls search different arrays
mcqs.explanation: Both calls run the identical binary search logic and complexity — the only variation is which half continues to be searched after a match is found, which determines whether the function converges on the first or last occurrence. Neither call has a duplicate-free requirement, and both operate on the same input array.

mcqs.question: What key property makes binary search still applicable to a rotated sorted array, even though the whole array isn't sorted?
options: Rotated arrays are always sorted if you ignore the first element
The rotation point is always exactly at the middle of the array
At least one of the two halves, split at any midpoint, is always properly sorted
Rotated arrays can only be searched with a linear scan, not binary search
mcqs.explanation: No matter where you split a rotated sorted array, one of the two resulting halves is guaranteed to still be in proper sorted order — that guarantee is what lets binary search identify which half to trust and search within. The rotation point can fall anywhere, not just the middle, and binary search absolutely does apply here, which is the entire point of this technique.

mcqs.question: To find the rotation point (minimum element's index) in a rotated sorted array with no duplicates, what comparison determines which half to search next?
options: Compare arr[lo] to target directly
Compare the array's total length to a fixed threshold
Always search the left half regardless of any comparison
Compare arr[mid] to arr[hi] — if arr[mid] > arr[hi], the minimum lies to the right of mid; otherwise it's at mid or to the left
mcqs.explanation: If arr[mid] is greater than arr[hi], the rotation break hasn't happened yet within [lo, mid], meaning the minimum must be further right; if arr[mid] <= arr[hi], the segment from mid to hi is already the sorted, un-rotated tail, so the minimum is at mid or earlier. There's no target involved in finding the rotation point itself, and neither a length threshold nor always searching left is a valid general strategy.

mcqs.question: A rotated sorted array with duplicates hits the case arr[lo] == arr[mid] == arr[hi]. What must the algorithm do, and what's the complexity consequence?
options: Shrink the window by one from each side (lo += 1, hi -= 1) and retry, since which half is sorted can't be determined from this comparison alone — this can degrade the worst case to O(n)
Always assume the left half is sorted in this case, preserving O(log n)
This case cannot occur if the array is genuinely rotated
Return immediately, since the target cannot exist in a uniform region
mcqs.explanation: When all three positions are equal, there's no way to tell which half contains the actual rotation point, forcing a one-at-a-time shrink instead of a confident halving — and in the worst case (an array of all-identical values), this repeats enough times to make the search effectively linear, a real and provable O(n) degradation. Assuming left-is-sorted would be an unjustified guess, this case absolutely can occur with duplicates, and the target might still exist within a uniform-looking region.

mcqs.question: An implementation of rotated-array search always assumes the right half is sorted and only ever checks the right half's range against the target. What's the consequence?
options: It works correctly on every rotation, since the right half is always sorted
It only fails when the array has duplicate elements
It produces wrong answers on rotations where the left half happens to be the sorted one, which is roughly half of all possible rotation points
It always throws an index-out-of-range error
mcqs.explanation: Which half is sorted alternates depending on where the rotation point falls relative to the current midpoint — hard-coding an assumption about which side is sorted, rather than checking explicitly, silently produces wrong results on the rotations where that assumption doesn't hold, while appearing to work on the others. This isn't specific to duplicates and doesn't cause an out-of-range error — it's a silent correctness bug across a real fraction of valid inputs.
